To view a copy of this licence, visit http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/ . Clear cell Carcinoma (ccRCC) is the most common and lethal subtype among renal cancers. In the present study we investigated the potential role of fatty acid-binding protein 4 (FABP4), also known as adipocyte FABP (A-FABP) or aP2 on ccRCC progression. Firstly, we found that FABP4 median serum levels were significantly higher in ccRCC patients compared to HD. Based on this result and to evaluate whether FABP4 plays a role on renal cancer malignant phenotype, we analyzed proliferation and migration in 786-O and ACHN cell lines using recombinant FABP4. We found that FABP4 significantly increased cell migration, whereas it had no significant effect on proliferation. As FABP4 is mainly expressed by adipocytes, we measured FABP4 adipocyte conditioned media (Ad-CM) levels showing that Ad-CM from ccRCC (Ad-CM ccRCC) had significantly higher mean values compared to Ad-CM obtained from Healthy Donors (HD). To assess the effects of adipocyte-released FABP-4, on cancer malignant phenotype we evaluated 786-O and ACHN proliferation and migration, using Ad-CM from ccRCC and Ad-CM from HD alone or in combination with FABP4 inhibitor BMS309403. Our results showed that Ad-CM enhanced cell proliferation in ACHN, but not in 786-O and on cell motility in both cell lines and this effect was partially reverted by BMS309403 in both cell lines. Moreover, in both cell lines, FABP4 effect was associated with an increased ERK phosphorylation. Collectively these data support the role of FABP4 in ccRCC progression and its potential use as noninvasive biomarker and therapeutic target for ccRCC. Keywords Adipocytes Renal cancer Peri-renal adipose tissue FABP4 issue-copyright-statement © BioMed Central Ltd., part of Springer Nature 2025 Introduction Renal carcinoma includes a heterogeneous group of malignancies from renal tubular epithelial cells that account for about 2.2% of all tumors and 1.8% of the total cancer mortality worldwide [ 1 ]. Generally, less than 10% of patients with RCC are diagnosed with the classic triad of flank pain, hematuria and palpable mass, more often the diagnosis occurs as incidental findings during ultrasonography or abdominal CT performed for another reason [ 2 ]. Accordingly, about 25% of patients present with distant metastatic disease at diagnosis [ 3 ]. Early detection of organ-confined RCC allows curative surgical resection via partial or radical nephrectomy and about 30% of patient who undergo surgical resection develop recurrence associated with high mortality rate [ 4 ]. Clear cell Renal Cell Carcinoma (ccRCC) is the most common and lethal subtype among renal cancers, comprising almost the 70% of cases [ 5 ]. Several epidemiological studies reported a strong association between perirenal adipose tissue (PRAT) thickness measured by computer tomography scan and ccRCC histotype in patients with renal cortical tumor [ 6 ]. In addition, it has been reported that PRAT width is associated with poor Progression Free Survival (PFS) [ 7 ] and Overall Survival (OS) in patients with surgical treated ccRCC [ 8 ]. These epidemiological data suggest that Peri-Renal Adipose Tissue (PRAT) may affect ccRCC behavior through the exchange of proteins, cytokines and metabolites with cancer cells [ 9 ], thanks to an extensive network of blood and lymph vessels connecting PRAT and ccRCC [ 10 ]. PRAT, in fact, is a peculiar visceral fat depot, defined along with pericardial Adipose Tissue (AT) and renal sinus fat an “ectopic fat” [ 11 ]. It is able to regulate kidney homeostasis in physiological conditions and involved in different metabolic diseases such as hypertension, atherosclerosis, and insulin resistance [ 12 ]. Thus, it is possible to speculate that peri-renal mature adipocytes may exert their effect on tumor microenvironment through secretion of adipokines and/or growth factors that support tumor progression. Although it is well known that high perirenal fat accumulation is associated with increased mortality and poor PFS of patients with localized ccRCC [ 7 , 8 ], the molecular mechanism underlying the relationship between perirenal adipocytes and ccRCC spread is still unclear. The discovery of extracellular FABP4 (e-FABP4) as adipocyte-released factor changed the game in research of a mechanistic link between cancer and AT. This small protein of 15 kDa is a fatty acid carrier, secreted by adipocytes, macrophages and endothelial cells, it is involved in metabolic disorders associated to visceral adiposity such as insulin resistance and atherosclerosis. Interestingly, e-FABP4 has been identified as driver of cell proliferation and migration in breast [ 13 ], colon [ 14 ], and ovarian cancer [ 15 ]. In the present study, we investigated the effect of FABP4 and adipocyte-released FABP4 on ccRCC cell proliferation and migration.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: ccRCC progression, cell migration, and proliferation; ERK phosphorylation; visceral adiposity; and peri-renal adipose tissue (PRAT) crosstalk with ccRCC cells. The investigation includes responses of human ccRCC cells (786-O and ACHN) to recombinant FABP4 and Adipocytes Conditioned Medium (Ad-CM) from ccRCC patients or healthy donors, with or without FABP4 inhibitor (BMS309403).
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: FABP4-mediated ERK phosphorylation promotes renal cancer cell migration. FABP4, secreted by adipocytes (including peri-renal mature adipocytes), functions as an adipokine/growth factor that supports tumor progression by enhancing cell proliferation (specifically in ACHN cells) and motility (in both 786-O and ACHN cell lines). This effect is strongly associated with increased ERK phosphorylation, which is pivotal in e-FABP4 signal transduction and can be mitigated by a FABP4 inhibitor. White visceral adipose tissue acts as an endocrine organ, releasing active compounds that promote the malignant phenotype and overall behavior of ccRCC cells. PRAT conditioned medium (CM) from ccRCC patients increases migration in ccRCC cell lines through the activation of the Wnt β-catenin pathway, with pERK and pPI3K identified as downstream mediators. FABP4, acting as a lipid chaperone, potentially transports free fatty acids from the tumor microenvironment to cancer cells. Additionally, FABP4 can influence cell proliferation by binding Desmoglein 2, leading to Erbin release and subsequent ERK phosphorylation. Adipocyte-released factors other than FABP4 may also contribute to ACHN cell proliferation.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: Recombinant FABP4 was utilized at a concentration of 10000 pg/mL in cell assays. The study compared the effects of recombinant FABP4 and adipocyte conditioned media (Ad-CM) from ccRCC patients versus healthy donors. The effects of Ad-CM on cell motility were partially reverted by the FABP4 inhibitor BMS309403, highlighting a pivotal role for FABP4. PRAT explants from ccRCC patients exhibited a browning process, which might explain their distinct secretory profile compared to PRAT from healthy donors.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: FABP4 specifically increased cell migration but had no significant effect on proliferation in 786-O and ACHN cell lines when recombinant FABP4 was directly applied. Conversely, Ad-CM enhanced proliferation in ACHN cells but not in 786-O. Serum FABP4 levels and e-FABP4 secretion from peri-renal adipocytes in ccRCC patients were significantly higher compared to healthy donors, and these differences were not influenced by common confounding factors such as BMI, Type 2 Diabetes, or hypertension, indicating specificity to ccRCC. The study isolated adipocytes from PRAT to specifically demonstrate that adipocyte-released FABP4 enhances ccRCC cancer cell motility, thus isolating its role from general adipose tissue explants.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Patients with clear cell Renal Cell Carcinoma (ccRCC), including those undergoing radical nephrectomy (35 subjects) and general cancer patients with abdominal cancers (e.g., ovarian, colorectal). Experiments involved human ccRCC cell lines (786-O and ACHN) and peri-renal adipocytes. Healthy donors (23 subjects) were included for comparison in clinical and in vitro studies.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: FABP4 supports ccRCC progression and is strongly associated with poorer Progression-Free Survival (PFS) and Overall Survival (OS) in the presence of high perirenal fat accumulation. Elevated circulating and urinary FABP4 serves as a biomarker associated with ccRCC. Extracellular FABP4, particularly from peri-renal adipocytes, contributes to ccRCC progression by promoting cancer cell migration and potentially proliferation (in ACHN cells) via mechanisms involving ERK phosphorylation. Visceral adiposity generally promotes tumor spread and affects the malignant phenotype of tumor cells. Early detection of organ-confined RCC enables curative surgical resection, but approximately 30% of patients experience recurrence, which is linked to high mortality.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: FABP4 demonstrates diagnostic utility as a potential noninvasive biomarker for ccRCC and prognostic utility for assessing recurrence risk. It also serves as a potential therapeutic target. High FABP4 levels and visceral adiposity are classified as adverse risk factors, contributing to tumor progression and negatively impacting OS and PFS.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: FABP4 is proposed as a potential noninvasive biomarker for ccRCC, with its extracellular form (e-FABP4) also identified as a driver of cell proliferation and migration in other cancers (breast, colon, ovarian), suggesting broad biological relevance. Serum FABP4 and e-FABP4 from peri-renal adipocytes are consistently elevated in ccRCC patients, independent of common confounding factors (BMI, Type 2 Diabetes, hypertension), which indicates good specificity. The in vitro functional role of e-FABP4 in enhancing cell migration and ERK phosphorylation supports its biological relevance. However, these data are primarily from in vitro models and require in vivo validation. Recombinant FABP4 showed no direct effect on proliferation, and Ad-CM-induced ACHN proliferation was not fully reverted by FABP4 inhibition, suggesting that other adipocyte-released factors also contribute to proliferation. Further studies on a larger patient population are necessary to assess the clinical benefit of FABP4 assessment in the management of ccRCC.
recommended_alternatives: Investigation of other adipocyte-released factors (as complementary factors)
